title: AQA GCSE Chemistry · Fuels and Feedstock

rounds.name: Carbon compounds as fuels and feedstock

items.stem: Crude oil is found in rocks. What was crude oil formed from?

options.text: The remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton
The remains of dinosaurs and other large animals buried in mud
The remains of ancient forests of land plants buried in swamp
Minerals in the rock that were changed by heat and pressure

items.why: This is exactly what the specification states: crude oil is the remains of an ancient biomass, mainly plankton, buried in mud.

items.stem: Why is crude oil described as a finite resource?

options.text: New oil is forming at the same rate that we use it
New crude oil forms far more slowly than we use it up
It is only found in a small number of countries on Earth
It is a mixture, so it cannot be put together again

items.why: A finite resource is one being consumed much faster than it is replaced, so supplies will run out.

items.stem: What is a hydrocarbon?

options.text: A molecule made of hydrogen, carbon and oxygen atoms
Any compound that contains carbon in its molecules
A molecule made of hydrogen and carbon atoms only
Any substance that burns to release energy

items.why: The specification defines hydrocarbons as molecules made up of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.

items.stem: Which statement about crude oil is correct?

options.text: It is one compound with a single fixed formula
It is a compound of carbon and hydrogen only
It is an element, as it comes from the ground
It is a mixture of a great many compounds

items.why: The specification says crude oil is a mixture of a very large number of compounds, most of them hydrocarbons.

items.stem: What is the general formula for the homologous series of alkanes?

options.text: CₙH₂ₙ — exactly twice as many hydrogens as carbons
CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — twice as many hydrogens as carbons, plus two
CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ — twice as many hydrogens as carbon, less two
CₙH₂ₙ₊₁ — twice the number of carbons, and one more

items.why: This is the general formula given in the specification; methane checks it, since 2 × 1 + 2 = 4.

items.stem: An alkane molecule contains 7 carbon atoms. What is its molecular formula?

options.text: C₇H₉, since 7 + 2 = 9
C₇H₁₅, from CₙH₂ₙ₊₁
C₇H₁₆, using CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
C₇H₁₄, using CₙH₂ₙ

items.why: With n = 7 the alkane formula gives 2 × 7 + 2 = 16 hydrogen atoms.

items.stem: What are the first four members of the alkanes, in order?

options.text: Methane, ethene, propene and butene
Methane, ethane, propane, pentane
Methane, ethane, butane, octane
Methane, ethane, propane, butane

items.why: These are the first four alkanes named by the specification, in order of increasing carbon number.

items.stem: An alkane can be shown as a molecular formula or as a displayed formula. What extra information does the displayed formula give?

options.text: It shows the bonds between the atoms
It shows how many atoms there are of each
It shows the charge on each of the atoms
It shows the mass of each atom present

items.why: A displayed formula shows every atom and every covalent bond, which a molecular formula cannot show.

items.stem: Ethane has the molecular formula C₂H₆. How many covalent bonds are shown in its displayed formula?

options.text: Eight, a C=C bond plus six C–H bonds
Six, just the six C–H bonds are drawn
Seven, one C–C bond plus six C–H bonds
Fourteen, the bonds counted at each atom

items.why: The two carbon atoms are joined by one bond, and each carbon holds three hydrogen atoms: 1 + 6 = 7.

items.stem: Which of these substances is an alkane?

options.text: C₅H₁₀ — hydrogen atoms = 2 × 5 exactly
C₅H₁₂O — it has 12 hydrogen atoms
C₄H₈ — it is also a hydrocarbon
C₅H₁₂ — hydrogen atoms = 2 × 5 + 2

items.why: It fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 5, so it is an alkane.

items.stem: Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation. What is the separation based on?

options.text: Differences in the boiling points of the molecules
Differences in how fast the molecules react together
Differences in the density of the liquid hydrocarbons
Differences in the colours of the compounds

items.why: Fractional distillation sorts hydrocarbons by the temperature at which their vapour condenses, which depends on boiling point.

items.stem: What do the molecules in one fraction of crude oil have in common?

options.text: They are all molecules of exactly the same compound
They have a similar number of carbon atoms
They all contain the same number of hydrogen atoms
They all have exactly the same boiling point

items.why: The specification defines a fraction as containing molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms.

items.stem: How does fractional distillation separate the hydrocarbons in crude oil?

options.text: The oil is melted, then each fraction freezes out at a different temperature
The oil is filtered, and the larger molecules are held by a fine mesh
The oil is burned, and the gases given off are then collected separately
The oil is evaporated, then each fraction condenses at a different temperature

items.why: Evaporation followed by condensation at different heights in the column is exactly how the specification requires this to be explained.

items.stem: Why are the fractions containing the largest molecules collected near the bottom of the column?

options.text: They have the highest boiling points, so they condense first
The bottom of the fractionating column is the coolest part of it
They are the densest, so they sink down to the bottom
They have the lowest boiling points of all fractions

items.why: The column is hottest at the bottom, so the fractions with the highest boiling points condense there.

items.stem: What are the fractions from crude oil processed to produce?

options.text: Fuels only, because every fraction is burned as a fuel
Fuels, and feedstock for the petrochemical industry
Fuels only, since feedstock is another word for fuel
Metals and ceramics used in the building trade

items.why: The specification states that the fractions can be processed to produce fuels and feedstock for the petrochemical industry.

items.stem: Which of these is a fuel produced from crude oil?

options.text: Charcoal, made by heating wood
Bioethanol, from fermentation
Kerosene, an aircraft fuel
Biodiesel, made from plant oils

items.why: Kerosene is one of the fuels the specification lists as produced from crude oil.

items.stem: Which of these are produced by the petrochemical industry?

options.text: Solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents
Petrol, diesel oil, kerosene and fuel oil
Limestone, cement, sand and glass items
Nitrogen, oxygen and argon, taken from air

items.why: These are the four examples of useful materials the specification gives for the petrochemical industry.

items.stem: Why is there such a vast array of natural and synthetic carbon compounds?

options.text: Carbon has far more isotopes than any other element does
Carbon atoms can form families of similar compounds
Carbon atoms bond ionically to form long chains
Carbon is the most abundant element in the Earth

items.why: The specification attributes the huge number of carbon compounds to carbon's ability to form families of similar compounds.

items.stem: Some properties of hydrocarbons depend on the size of their molecules. Which set of properties is this?

options.text: Boiling point, solubility and conductivity
Colour, density and electrical conductivity
Boiling point, viscosity and flammability
Density, hardness and melting point

items.why: These are the three properties the specification names as depending on molecular size.

items.stem: How do the properties of hydrocarbons change as the molecules get larger?

options.text: Boiling point down, viscosity up, flammability down
Boiling point rises, viscosity down, flammability up
Boiling point falls, viscosity falls, flammability up
Boiling point up, viscosity up, flammability down

items.why: Larger molecules attract each other more strongly, so they boil higher and flow less easily, and they are harder to ignite.

items.stem: How does the boiling point of a hydrocarbon change as its molecules get larger?

options.text: It decreases, as larger molecules are heavier and move slower
It increases, as larger molecules attract each other more strongly
It stays the same, since size only affects density
It rises at first and then falls again for long chains

items.why: More energy is needed to separate larger molecules, so the boiling point rises with molecular size.

items.stem: How does the viscosity of a hydrocarbon change as its molecules get larger?

options.text: It increases, so the liquid catches fire faster
It decreases, so the liquid flows freely
It increases, so the liquid flows less easily
It is the same for all liquid hydrocarbons

items.why: Longer molecules attract and tangle with each other more, so thick fractions pour very slowly.

items.stem: How does the flammability of a hydrocarbon change as its molecules get larger?

options.text: It increases, as there is more carbon to burn
It increases, so it is easier to set alight
It does not change for any hydrocarbon
It decreases, so it is harder to ignite

items.why: Large molecules are hard to vaporise, and a fuel must vaporise before it will burn.

items.stem: Liquefied petroleum gases are used in portable camping stoves. Which property makes them suitable?

options.text: They are highly flammable and ignite very easily
They have high boiling points and do not evaporate
They are very viscous and pour out slowly and safely
They contain the largest hydrocarbon molecules of all

items.why: Small hydrocarbon molecules vaporise readily and are highly flammable, which is exactly what a small stove needs.

items.stem: What happens when a hydrocarbon undergoes complete combustion?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen form, and energy is taken in
Carbon monoxide and water form, and energy is released
Carbon dioxide and water form, and heat energy is released
Carbon dioxide and water form, and energy is taken in

items.why: The specification states that complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water, and that combustion releases energy.

items.stem: During the combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel, what happens to the carbon and the hydrogen?

options.text: Only the carbon is oxidised, not the hydrogen
Both are reduced, because both lose oxygen
Only carbon dioxide forms, and no water
Both are oxidised, because both gain oxygen

items.why: The carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen is oxidised to water, so both gain oxygen.

items.stem: Which equation shows the complete combustion of methane, CH₄?

options.text: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 4H₂O
2CH₄ + 4O₂ → CO₂ + 4H₂O
CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O

items.why: Carbon: 1 and 1. Hydrogen: 4 and 4. Oxygen: 4 and 4. The equation is balanced.

items.stem: Which equation shows the complete combustion of propane, C₃H₈?

options.text: 2C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 6CO₂ + 8H₂O
C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
2C₃H₈ + 10O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
2C₃H₈ + 10O₂ → 6CO₂ + 10H₂O

items.why: Carbon: 3 and 3. Hydrogen: 8 and 8. Oxygen: 10 and 10. The equation is balanced.

items.stem: Ethane has the formula C₂H₆. Which equation shows its complete combustion?

options.text: C₂H₆ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
C₂H₆ + O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O

items.why: Carbon: 4 and 4. Hydrogen: 12 and 12. Oxygen: 14 and 14. Doubling the ethane avoids a half-molecule of oxygen.

items.stem: What happens to hydrocarbon molecules during cracking?

options.text: They are broken down into smaller, more useful molecules
They are separated from one another without being changed
They are joined together to make much larger molecules
They are burned to release energy and carbon dioxide

items.why: The specification defines cracking as breaking hydrocarbons down to produce smaller, more useful molecules.

items.stem: Why are the fractions with the largest molecules cracked?

options.text: Fuels made of large molecules are in much higher demand
There is a high demand for fuels with small molecules
It is the only way to remove the sulfur from these fuels
It turns each fraction into one pure single compound

items.why: Cracking converts a surplus of long-chain molecules into short-chain fuels that are in high demand.

items.stem: Which two methods of cracking does the specification name?

options.text: Catalytic cracking and fractional cracking
Steam cracking and electrolytic cracking
Catalytic cracking and steam cracking
Thermal cracking and pressure cracking

items.why: These are the two methods the specification names.

items.stem: What conditions are used for catalytic cracking?

options.text: Hydrocarbons are vaporised and passed over a hot catalyst
Hydrocarbons are vaporised and mixed with steam only
Hydrocarbons are cooled and poured over a cold catalyst
Hydrocarbons are dissolved in water with a catalyst

items.why: In catalytic cracking the hydrocarbon is turned into a vapour and passed over a hot catalyst.

items.stem: What conditions are used for steam cracking?

options.text: The vapour is mixed with steam and then passed over a hot catalyst bed
The vapour is mixed with steam and heated to a very high temperature
The vapour is mixed with steam and kept at a mild temperature
The liquid is mixed with water and warmed gently in a flask

items.why: Steam cracking mixes hydrocarbon vapour with steam and heats it to a very high temperature, with no catalyst.

items.stem: The products of cracking include alkanes. What is the other type of hydrocarbon produced?

options.text: Only more alkanes, but smaller in size
Alcohols, that contain oxygen as well
Alkenes, a more reactive hydrocarbon
Polymers, made of very long chains

items.why: The specification states that the products of cracking include alkanes and another type of hydrocarbon called alkenes.

items.stem: How can you show that a hydrocarbon is an alkene and not an alkane?

options.text: Add bromine water; both will react
Add bromine water; the alkane just reacts slower
Add a lit splint and listen for the pop
Add bromine water and shake well

items.why: Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes and react with bromine water, which is why it is used as the test.

items.stem: What colour change is seen when bromine water reacts with an alkene?

options.text: Colourless bromine water turns orange in colour
Orange bromine water is decolourised to colourless
Orange bromine water turns a cloudy white colour
Orange bromine water turns a blue-black colour

items.why: Bromine water starts orange, and the alkene reacts with the bromine so the colour disappears.

items.stem: What are alkenes used for?

options.text: Only as fuels for cars, lorries and aeroplanes
Nothing much, as polymers come from alkanes
To produce polymers and many other chemicals
To make metals and ceramic building parts

items.why: The specification states that alkenes are used to produce polymers and as starting materials for many other chemicals.

items.stem: Cracking one molecule of C₁₀H₂₂ produces one molecule of C₂H₄. What is the other product?

options.text: C₈H₁₆, treating the alkane as CₙH₂ₙ
C₁₀H₁₈, since only hydrogen is removed
C₁₂H₂₆, adding the two formulae up
C₈H₁₈, so that all the atoms balance

items.why: Carbon: 10 = 8 + 2. Hydrogen: 22 = 18 + 4. The equation balances.

items.stem: Give one reason why cracking is useful.

options.text: It turns surplus large molecules into fuels
It makes crude oil into a renewable resource
It removes all of the carbon dioxide from fuel
It joins up small molecules to make long chains

items.why: Cracking converts long-chain fractions that are in low demand into short-chain fuels that are in high demand.
